sovereignty-challenges-s1.title: What five supranational organizations do
sovereignty-challenges-s1.source: Summarized by LevlPrep from each organization's founding treaty and official website, read November 2026

table.caption: Main functions of five supranational organizations (founding year in brackets)
rows: Peace, security and cooperation among states
To carry out decisions of the Security Council
To treat an armed attack on one member as an attack on all
Single market, shared laws and, for most members, one currency
To follow EU laws and EU court rulings in shared areas; free movement of people
Peace, security and development in Africa
That the union may step in to stop genocide or war crimes; a member can be suspended after a coup
Protecting the Arctic environment and the lives of its peoples
To work by agreement of all eight Arctic states, with Indigenous peoples' groups at the table

sovereignty-challenges-s2.title: Four states and how they changed

map.label: Reference map of the world with four states marked: A in southwestern Europe, B in northern North America, C in West Africa, D in Central Asia

items.q: According to the table, which organization exists mainly for shared military defense?
options: NATO
The European Union
The Arctic Council
The African Union

why.correct: Read the "Main function" column: NATO is the military alliance for shared defense.
options: Right: NATO is a military alliance: an attack on one member counts as an attack on all.
The EU's main functions are its single market and shared laws.
The Arctic Council works on the Arctic environment and its peoples.
The African Union works on peace and development, not a shared army of all members.

items.q: Which organization in the table asks its members to follow laws made by shared bodies and rulings of a shared court?
options: NATO
The Arctic Council
The United Nations
The European Union

why.correct: The EU goes furthest in pooling sovereignty: in its shared areas, EU law applies in every member state.
options: NATO members agree on shared defense, not shared laws.
The Arctic Council works by agreement of all eight states.
UN members agree to carry out Security Council decisions, not to follow a body of shared laws.
Right: EU members follow EU laws and EU court rulings in shared areas.

items.q: Which organization in the table limits its members' sovereignty the least, according to what members agree to?
options: The European Union
The African Union
The Arctic Council
NATO

why.correct: An organization that acts by agreement of all its members leaves each one able to say no, so it limits sovereignty little.
options: EU members follow shared laws and court rulings.
The union may step in and can suspend members.
Right: It works by agreement of all eight states, so each can block a decision.
NATO members commit to defend each other.

items.q: What can a student NOT learn from this table?
options: Which organization deals with Arctic issues
How many states each organization has
Which organization is a military alliance
In which year the African Union was founded

why.correct: The table describes what each body does. Membership changes over time, so learn what each organization does, not how many members it has.
options: The Arctic Council row shows that.
Right: The table lists functions, not membership counts.
The NATO row shows that.
The table gives 2002.

items.q: In 1999, a new territory was created in the north of the state at mark B, governed mostly by and for Inuit. Which state is it?
options: Canada
Spain
Kazakhstan
Nigeria

why.correct: Nunavut, in northern Canada, gives Inuit, most of its people, a government of their own inside Canada: devolution to a subnational unit.
options: Right: Mark B is in northern Canada, where Nunavut was created in 1999.
Spain is at mark A, in Europe.
Kazakhstan is at mark D, in Central Asia.
Nigeria is at mark C, in West Africa.

items.q: Which marked state became independent when the Soviet Union broke apart in 1991?
options: Mark A
Mark B
Mark C
Mark D

why.correct: Kazakhstan (mark D) is one of the 15 states formed when the Soviet Union broke apart: devolution all the way to new states.
options: Mark A is Spain, independent for centuries.
Mark B is in Canada.
Mark C is Nigeria, independent from Britain in 1960.
Right: Mark D is Kazakhstan, one of the 15 states that came out of the Soviet Union.

items.q: The states at marks A and C both answered regional pressure by sharing power with subnational units, but did not break apart. What does this show?
options: Devolution leads to a breakup in each case
Both states became unitary to stop devolution
Devolution can keep a state together by giving regions self-rule
Both states joined NATO to end regional pressure

why.correct: Spain (mark A) created autonomous communities after 1978, and Nigeria (mark C) grew from 12 states in 1967 to 36 by 1996. Giving regions power can ease pressure to leave.
options: Spain and Nigeria are still single states.
Both moved power toward regions, not away from them.
Right: Spain's autonomous communities and Nigeria's states give regions power inside one state.
Nigeria is not in NATO, and NATO is about defense.
A region breaking away from its state
Three or more states joining an organization for shared goals
A people seeking a state of its own
A state taking land where its people live

why.correct: Supranationalism is cooperation among three or more states through an organization for shared goals, such as defense, trade or the environment, in which members give up some sovereignty.
options: That is devolution, the opposite direction.
Right: Members share some decisions, so each gives up a little sovereignty.
That is self-determination or separatism.
That is irredentism.

items.q: In the 1990s, Yugoslavia broke apart into several smaller states, often after wars between them. What is this process called?
options: Balkanization
Supranationalism
Democratization
Reapportionment

why.correct: Balkanization is the breakup of a region or state into smaller states that are often hostile to each other. It is named for the Balkans in southeastern Europe.
options: Right: The breakup of a region into smaller, often hostile states is named for the Balkans.
Supranationalism brings states together; this split one apart.
Democratization is the spread of democratic government.
Reapportionment shares out seats in a legislature.

items.q: In Tunisia in 2010 and 2011, protesters used mobile phones and social media to share news and plan marches, and the long-time ruler left power. Which process did communication technology help?
options: Balkanization
Irredentism
Ethnic cleansing
Democratization

why.correct: Communication technology can help democratization (and also devolution and supranational cooperation) by letting people share information and organize across space.
options: Tunisia did not break into smaller states.
No neighboring state claimed Tunisian land.
The protests did not remove an ethnic group.
Right: The spread of democratic government was helped by fast, shared news.

items.q: In 2011, after decades of conflict, people in southern Sudan voted to leave Sudan, and South Sudan became independent. What does this show?
options: Supranationalism making a state larger
A unitary state becoming federal
Devolution can end in a breakup of the state
Irredentism by a neighboring state

why.correct: At its furthest, devolution breaks a state apart. Sudan in 2011 and the Soviet Union in 1991 are two examples of state breakup.
options: Sudan became smaller, not part of a larger body.
Sudan split; it did not just share power.
Right: Power moved so far to the region that it became its own state.
The push came from people inside Sudan.

items.q: In 2016, 51.9% of UK voters chose to leave the European Union, and the UK left in 2020. Supporters of leaving often said they wanted to "take back control." What were they reacting to?
options: NATO's control over the British army and navy
Limits the EU puts on a member's sovereignty
The UN's control of UK elections
The Arctic Council's rules on British cities

why.correct: Supranational membership brings benefits, such as a large shared market, but limits sovereignty. In the UK, a majority decided the costs were too high; 48.1% voted to stay.
options: NATO does not run its members' armies.
Right: EU members follow shared laws and allow free movement of people.
The UN does not run UK elections.
The Arctic Council does not make rules for cities.

items.q: When soldiers take power in a coup in an African state, the African Union often suspends that state from the union until elected government returns. How does this affect sovereignty?
options: Members accept outside judgment of their rulers
It makes the suspended state fully independent of the rest of Africa
It turns the suspended state into a federal state
It gives the union control of the state's army

why.correct: Supranational bodies can limit sovereignty: members agree to rules about how they govern, and to penalties when they break them.
options: Right: Joining the union means accepting penalties for breaking its rules.
Suspension does not change a state's borders or independence.
Suspension does not change a state's form of government.
The union suspends; it does not take over armies.

items.q: How do supranationalism and devolution both challenge a state's sovereignty?
options: Both move power from regions up to the national government in the capital
Both make a state larger by adding territory
Both remove the national government from power
One shares power up to groups of states, the other down to regions

why.correct: Supranationalism moves some decisions up to organizations such as the EU; devolution moves some down to regions such as Scotland. Either way, the national government decides less alone.
options: Both move power away from the national government.
Neither adds territory.
National governments remain in both cases.
Right: Both leave the national government deciding less on its own.

items.q: Which are reasons states join supranational organizations? Select all that apply.
options: To deal with problems that cross borders, such as pollution or disease
To defend each other against attack
To gain a bigger market for their goods and services
To gain full control over their own laws
To redraw their internal voting districts
To end their membership in the United Nations

why.correct: States join for security, for larger markets and to face global problems together, and pay for it with some sovereignty.
options: Right: One state cannot clean a shared sea alone.
Right: Alliances such as NATO pool defense.
Right: A shared market lets firms sell to more people at lower cost.
Joining usually means sharing some lawmaking, not gaining control.
Voting districts are a national matter.
Joining other bodies does not end UN membership.

items.q: Build an explanation of one gain and one cost of joining a supranational organization.

why.correct: Name the organization, then what members gain and what they give up, with the link.

specific.frame: By joining ___, a state gains ___, but ___.
specific.model: By joining the European Union, a state gains free movement of goods and people in a single market, but it must follow EU laws in shared areas, so its own parliament decides less on its own.

place.label: Organization
options: the European Union
an organization

cause.label: Gain
options: free movement of goods and people in a single market
control over the laws of other members

why.1: Members share lawmaking; no one member controls the others.

effect.label: Cost
options: it must follow EU laws in shared areas, so its own parliament decides less on its own
it loses its seat at the United Nations

why.1: EU members keep their UN seats.
